title: Tensor base change preserves larger ideal-power quotients under a finite-level scalar congruence
statement: Let $R,B,C$ be commutative rings, with $R$-algebra structure maps $\iota:R\to B$ and $\rho:R\to C$. Let $I\subseteq R$ and $J\subseteq C$ be ideals with $IC\subseteq J$, where extension denotes the ideal generated by the image. Fix an integer $n\geq1$. Suppose there is a surjective $R$-algebra map $\pi:B\to R/I^n$ with $\pi\iota$ the quotient map and $\ker\pi=I^nB$. Put $D=C\otimes_RB$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], with multiplication $(c\otimes b)(c'\otimes b')=cc'\otimes bb'$ and unit $1\otimes1$, and put $f(c)=c\otimes1$. Then the canonical ring map $\alpha:C/J^n\to D/J^nD$, $[c]\mapsto[f(c)]$, is an isomorphism. If $\bar\rho:R/I^n\to C/J^n$ is induced by $\rho$, its inverse satisfies $\alpha^{-1}([c\otimes b])=[c]\,\bar\rho(\pi(b))$ for every $c\in C$, $b\in B$.

proof.text: Write $K=J^n$ and $E=C/K$. Each element of $I^n$ is a finite sum of multiples of products of $n$ elements of $I$. Since $\rho(I)\subseteq J$, their images lie in $K$. Thus $\bar\rho([r])=[\rho(r)]$ is well-defined: changing $r$ by an element of $I^n$ changes its image by an element of $K$. It preserves sums, products and the unit by the same formulas on representatives. Let $q:C\to E$ be the quotient homomorphism.

source.place: Tag 00CX (lemma-tensor-product), bilinearity relations and generation by pure tensors; explicit quotient calculation.

proof.text: Put $g=\bar\rho\circ\pi:B\to E$. It is an $R$-algebra homomorphism, since $g(\iota(r))=[\rho(r)]$. Apply the tensor-algebra universal property to $q$ and $g$. It gives an $R$-algebra homomorphism $h:D\to E$ with $h(c\otimes b)=[c]g(b)$. The same cited statement makes $f(c)=c\otimes1$ a ring homomorphism, and $h\circ f=q$.

proof.text: On a representative $[c]\in E$, $\beta\alpha([c])=h(c\otimes1)=[c]$. On a pure tensor class, $\alpha\beta([c\otimes b])=\alpha([c]\bar\rho(\pi(b)))=[c\otimes b]$ by Step 4. Every element of $D$ is a finite sum of pure tensors (absorb any $R$-coefficient into the first factor), so additivity proves $\alpha\beta=\mathrm{id}$ on $D/KD$. Thus $\alpha$ is an isomorphism with inverse $\beta$; the formula for $h$ in Step 2 gives exactly the asserted inverse formula.
